title: Our Ancient Ancestors’ Lost Habitat Revealed by 700,000-Year-Old Elephant’s Tooth - Nautilus
gist: A roughly 700,000-year-old elephant tooth found with basalt hand axes at the Daughters of Jacob Bridge site near Israel's Hula Valley is being used to reconstruct the Levant's paleoclimate. A Haifa University-led team applied CT scans, 3D reconstruction and isotopic analysis, publishing in Quaternary Science Reviews.

insights.claim: Around a million years ago the Levant, the narrow land bridge linking Africa to Eurasia, served as a heavily used corridor for ancient hominins, most likely Homo erectus and Homo heidelbergensis, who settled there.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Background context only; illustrates how geography shapes long-run migration routes.
insights.quote: the narrow land bridge linking Africa to Eurasia proved to be a popular thoroughfare for other ancient hominins who settled in the region
insights.locator: The Levant was a busy corridor

insights.claim: Much about the paleoclimate of the Levant during the period of early hominin settlement remains unknown.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Highlights a data gap that new analytical techniques are starting to fill.
insights.quote: there’s still a lot we don’t know about the paleoclimate there
insights.locator: The Levant was a busy corridor

insights.claim: An elephant tooth dated to about 700,000 years ago was found alongside tusk fragments and a cache of basalt hand axes in the Daughters of Jacob Bridge region just south of Israel's Hula Valley.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Co-located fauna and tools let researchers link environmental conditions directly to hominin activity.
insights.quote: The tooth, dated to around 700,000 years ago, was discovered alongside tusk fragments and a cache of basalt hand axes from the same period

insights.claim: A Haifa University-led team used CT scans, 3D reconstruction and isotopic analysis on a 700,000-year-old elephant tooth to infer the Levant's ancient climate, publishing results in Quaternary Science Reviews.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Shows imaging and isotope tools turning single fossils into climate proxies, a niche demand driver for scientific instrumentation.
